text.p: Following are highlights of the main stories in Croatian newspapers on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified them and does not vouch for their accuracy.
VJESNIK

- Croatian President Franjo Tudjman was sworn in for his second five-year term on Tuesday. He vowed to be an impartial president of all Croatian citizens, and said economic growth has to reach 6-7 percent in order to increase the living standard and social security of all employed.

- Croatian oil monopoly INA took over its petrol stations in the Serb-controlled region of Eastern Slavonia which the local Serb authorities expropriated in 1991 when they rebelled against Croatia's declaration of independence from former Yugoslavia. Most of the 15 stations in the region that is to come back under full government control in January were damaged.
- Celebration of "Homeland Thanksgiving Day" -- the second anniversary of the Croatian army capture of the rebel Serb capital Knin during Operation Storm -- took place around the country.

- U.S. envoys Robert Gelbard and Richard Holbrooke will threaten Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic with a new round of trade sanctions if he does not stick to the committments made under the 1995 Dayton peace plan.

- Political sources say Wednesday's summit between Croatian President Franjo Tudjman and the chairman of the Bosnian collective presidency Alija Izetbegovic in Split comes at a crucial moment for the Dayton peace agreement, which each side interpretes in a way that suits its interests.
- Some 170,000 tourists are currently staying in Istria, 107,000 in the Rijeka area, and some 96,000 in Split-Zadar area of central Dalmatia.
VECERNJI LIST

- Tudjman sworn in as president, Vecernji singles out his vow that he was not prepared for any compromise that would threaten Croatian national interests and to work to remove the remnants of the former communist system in the government.

- Croatian army pilot, Rudolf Peresin, whose plane was shot down over Bosanska Gradiska in May 1995, was captured alive, claims one of the negotiators in Peresin's case. Bosnian Serbs have recently delivered Peresin's remains to Zagreb.

- Croatian Hoteliers Association said in a statement that continued and much publicised polemics over the new slogan of the Croatian tourist board -- "Croatia, Paradise on Earth" -- was not serving Croatian tourism's best interest.

- Two largest private grocery chains, Konzum and Diona, said they would start raising prices as of next week in order to make up for losses due to illegal competition. The Croatian retail market is in chaos, heads of the chains said.
- The second biggest Croatian stock exchange, the informal Varazdin OTC market, complains against the decision of the Zagreb Bourse to scrap its commission, branding it as "unfair".
- The government completed a two-year rehauling programme in six out of 14 loss-making firms of special interest, but the firms themselves do not feel they can stand on their own feet completely yet.

- Agriculture ministry was instrumental in the recent government decision to raise taxes for 48 agricultural products, including milk, cheese, tomato, peppers etc. "While my colleague, Economy Minister Nenad Porges is for complete liberalisation, I am for complete protectionsim," said Agriculture Minister Ivan Dominikovic in an interview.
- Istrian hotelier Rivijera Holding in Porec expects two million overnights, or 20 percent up on 1996, and net profit of 15.6 million kuna this year.
- Private accommodation -- also known as "Zimmer Frei" for the simple way of advertising its services -- is coming back in a big way on the Croatian Adriatic coast.
SLOBODNA DALMACIJA
- Tudjman vows to spare no effort in the rebuilding and development of the country in his second term as president.
- Interview with the government's refugee office head Lovre Pejkovic: Many more Serbs returned to Croatia than the number of Croats allowed to return to their homes in Eastern Slavonia.

- Situation in Jajce calms down after last weekend's incidents when Bosnian Croats prevented Moslem refugees from returning to their homes. Croat authorities in central Bosnia condemned such behaviour but warned that unplanned and unannounced return could have grave consequences. -- Davor Huic, Zagreb newsroom +385 1 455 7075
